title: Topological Sort and Cycle Detection
excerpt: Given a pile of tasks with dependencies, find an order that respects all of them. The algorithm is what you would do by hand, and it detects the impossible cases for free.
seoTitle: Topological Sort: Kahn's Algorithm and Cycle Detection
seoDescription: Topological sorting derived: why a cycle makes ordering impossible, how in-degree counting gives Kahn's algorithm, a full trace, the DFS finish-time alternative, and why the output is rarely unique.

content.text: You have a pile of things to do and some of them depend on others. Compile this file before that one. Take the prerequisite before the course. Put your socks on before your shoes. The question is whether there is an order that respects every constraint, and if so, what it is.
Written as a graph, each task is a node and each edge points from a thing to a thing that must come after it. Producing a valid order is called
topological sorting
, and it is one of the most directly useful algorithms in this section, because the answer is a build plan, a schedule or an install order.

body.text: When an answer exists at all

content.text: Before finding an order it is worth asking when one exists, because the answer is clean and it drives the algorithm.

Suppose the graph has a cycle: A before B, B before C, C before A. Any ordering has to put one of the three first, and whichever you pick has something in the cycle that must come before it. So no order exists, and no cleverness will produce one.

The other direction holds too. If the graph has no directed cycle then an order always exists. So the question "can these tasks be scheduled" and the question "is this graph a DAG" are the same question, which is why the previous page bothered to name DAGs.

Think about what you would do by hand with a real to-do list. You would look for something with nothing blocking it, do that, cross it off, and notice that crossing it off may have unblocked other things. Then repeat.
That instinct is the algorithm, and it needs only one number per node, how many things are still blocking it, a count called the node's in-degree: the number of edges pointing at it.

A node with in-degree 0 has nothing waiting on it, so it is safe to emit. Emitting it removes its outgoing edges, which lowers the in-degree of everything it pointed at, which may drop some of them to 0 and make them available in turn. Keep a collection of the currently-available nodes so you do not have to rescan for them.

This is Kahn's algorithm, and the pleasant part is the cycle check. You never have to look for a cycle explicitly. If you finish and have emitted fewer nodes than the graph contains, whatever is left is stuck behind something, and stuck means a cycle. The count is the detector.
Same dependencies as the previous page: shirt before tie, shirt before belt, trousers before belt, trousers before shoes, socks before shoes, tie before jacket.

body.code:
in-degrees at the start
  shirt 0   trousers 0   socks 0   tie 1   belt 2   shoes 2   jacket 1

ready queue [shirt, trousers, socks]

take shirt     output: shirt
  tie    2 -> ... 1 -> 0   ready
  belt   2 -> 1
take trousers  output: shirt, trousers
  belt   1 -> 0   ready
  shoes  2 -> 1
take socks     output: shirt, trousers, socks
  shoes  1 -> 0   ready
take tie       output: ... tie        jacket 1 -> 0   ready
take belt      output: ... belt
take shoes     output: ... shoes
take jacket    output: ... jacket

7 nodes emitted, 7 nodes in the graph, so there was no cycle.

content.text: Notice that there were three nodes available at the very start, and the algorithm had to pick one. A different pick gives a different valid order. Topological orders are usually not unique, and a problem that expects one specific answer has to say which tie-break to use. If you need the lexicographically smallest order, make the ready collection a min-heap instead of a plain list, and the rest is unchanged.
Switch to the DAG tab. Every arrow means "must come before", so a node cannot be taken until every arrow pointing at it has been dealt with.

body.text: The other way to do it

content.text: There is a second method worth knowing, because it costs nothing once you have depth-first search and it shows up in a lot of published code.
Run a DFS. When a node
finishes
, meaning you have fully explored everything reachable from it, push it onto a list. At the end, reverse the list.

The reason that works is worth a moment. A node cannot finish until everything downstream of it has finished, so it always lands earlier in the finish list than its dependents. Reversing puts it after them, which is exactly the ordering you want. Detecting cycles takes one extra piece of state: if the DFS ever meets an edge back to a node that is currently open, meaning you are still inside its call, that is a cycle.

Kahn's version is usually easier to reason about and gives you the cycle check for free. The DFS version is more compact if you already have a DFS in front of you and do not want the in-degree bookkeeping. Both cost
O(V + E)

variants.code:
from collections import deque

def topological_sort(node_count, edges):
    adj = [[] for _ in range(node_count)]
    in_degree = [0] * node_count

    for before, after in edges:
        adj[before].append(after)
        in_degree[after] += 1          # one more thing blocking it

    ready = deque(v for v in range(node_count) if in_degree[v] == 0)

    order = []
    while ready:
        v = ready.popleft()
        order.append(v)
        for nxt in adj[v]:
            in_degree[nxt] -= 1
            if in_degree[nxt] == 0:
                ready.append(nxt)

    # Anything left un-emitted is stuck behind a cycle.
    return order if len(order) == node_count else None

content.text: Returning
null

rather than a partial order is deliberate. A half-finished topological order is not a useful object, and callers that silently use one will produce a build that fails much later for reasons that look unrelated.
Pointing the edges the wrong way.

If an edge from A to B means "A depends on B" rather than "A must come before B", your output comes out exactly reversed. Both conventions exist in the wild, so decide which one you are using and write it down next to the code.
Assuming the order is unique.
It usually is not. Tests that compare against one specific expected order will fail on a perfectly correct implementation unless the problem pinned down a tie-break.
Skipping the count check.
Without it, a graph with a cycle returns a short list that looks like a valid order until something downstream breaks.
Forgetting isolated nodes.

A task with no dependencies in either direction has in-degree 0 and belongs in the output. If you seed the ready collection from the edge list rather than from every node, those nodes vanish silently.

questions.prompt: Kahn's algorithm emits 6 nodes on a graph with 8. What does that mean?

options.label: The remaining 2 are in or behind a cycle, so no valid order exists
The ready queue was drained too early
Two nodes had no outgoing edges

questions.prompt: What is a node's in-degree, in this context?

options.label: How many things must still be completed before it becomes available
How many tasks depend on it
Its position in the final order

questions.prompt: Your topological sort is correct but the grader rejects it. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: Several valid orders exist and the grader wanted one particular tie-break
In-degrees were computed on the wrong nodes

questions.prompt: In the DFS version, why does reversing the finish order give a valid topological order?

options.label: A node cannot finish until everything downstream of it has finished, so reversing puts it before them
DFS visits nodes in order of in-degree
The finish order is already correct and reversing is a convention
